items.prompt: What's the core distinction this unit draws between an IC's job and a manager's job?
choices: Managers work longer hours than ICs

An IC's unit of output is their own work; a manager's unit of output is the output of the people they manage -- a manager who's personally the top performer while their team is unclear or unsupported is failing at the actual job
There is no real distinction -- management is just IC work with more meetings
Managers are only responsible for hiring, not for team output
items.explanation: The unit explicitly reframes the manager's job around a different output equation: the team's collective effectiveness, not the manager's personal work product. Personal technical excellence stops being the measure of success once the role changes, even though it's the skill that likely earned the promotion.
items.reference:
IC output

Own effort x own skill

Manager output

Sum across the team of (effort x skill x support)

Why: a manager who's personally the top performer while the team is unclear or unsupported is failing at the job, regardless of personal output.
items.learnMore:
Two different output equations

An IC's output is direct, visible, and entirely within their own control. A manager's output routes through other people, which means it's indirect, often invisible day to day, and mostly not within their direct control.

The manager equation has a term the IC equation doesn't: how well-supported each person is. Closing gaps in that term is now the actual job, even though it produces no code of its own.

items.prompt: Why does the "retreat to IC work" failure mode happen so commonly to new managers, per L2?
choices: New managers are usually lazy about learning new skills

The familiar IC work is genuinely productive and provides fast, comfortable feedback, which makes it an easy default under the uncertainty of unfamiliar management tasks -- even though it withholds capacity only the manager can provide
Companies explicitly instruct new managers to keep doing IC work
It only happens to managers who were mediocre ICs before promotion
items.explanation: L2's equation model makes this explicit: familiar, well-understood IC work feels like real progress and IS productive, which is precisely what makes it an easy retreat under the discomfort of unclear management tasks like a hard feedback conversation or a political prioritization call.
items.reference:
Why the retreat happens

Fast Familiar IC work: fast feedback, feels like real progress
Slow Unblocking/coaching/politics: unfamiliar, uncomfortable, slow
Gap Only the manager can do the uncomfortable tasks

Why: the comfortable option is genuinely productive, which is exactly what makes it an easy, invisible default under pressure.
items.learnMore:
The retreat-to-IC-work trap

A new manager's actual to-do list is full of unfamiliar, uncomfortable work: unblocking an ambiguous requirement, a hard feedback conversation, a cross-team priority call. Sitting right next to that list is a familiar alternative the manager already knows how to do well.

Every uncomfortable task is something only the manager is positioned to do -- the org gave them the context, authority, or relationship for it. The familiar task, however well done, is something a senior IC on the team could likely have done too.

Common mistake

Assuming this only happens to lazy or mediocre managers. It happens to skilled, hardworking ones precisely because the familiar work is genuinely good work -- that's what makes it such an easy trap.

The bug fix is genuinely good, fast-feedback work the manager already knows how to do well -- which is exactly what makes it a more comfortable default than the unfamiliar, slower-feedback meeting only the manager can run
Prioritization meetings are never actually necessary
The manager is deliberately sabotaging the team

items.prompt: This unit describes the IC-to-manager shift as moving from a "multiplier of one" to a "multiplier of many." What does that mean?
choices: Managers should literally multiply their working hours by the team size
An IC's leverage is their own effort alone; a manager's leverage is how much they can lift the collective effort of everyone on the team, even by a small amount each
It means managers get paid multiple salaries
It's a metaphor with no practical meaning
items.explanation: A manager who makes several people meaningfully more effective has produced more total value than personally doing a fraction of one person's work -- even though the team-wide lift is far less visible day to day than a personal deliverable.
items.reference:
Multiplier of one

Your own effort, alone

Multiplier of many

A team's collective effort, shifted by your support

Why: a manager who makes four people 10% more effective produces more real value than personally shipping a few extra PRs -- even though only the PRs show up on a dashboard.
items.learnMore:
Multiplier of one vs. multiplier of many

As an IC, the only lever you have is your own effort and skill. As a manager, your real lever is how much you can multiply everyone else's effort -- through clearer priorities, better coaching, and removing blockers.

This is why manager impact is genuinely harder to see week to week: a 10% lift applied across four people is real and large, but it's distributed and delayed, not a single visible artifact like a merged PR.

Common mistake

Concluding that because manager impact is invisible, it must be smaller than IC impact. Distributed impact across a team is very often larger in total value than any one person's individual output -- it's just harder to point at.

items.prompt: Why might a manager who makes their whole team modestly more effective be creating more real value than one who personally ships a large amount of code?
choices: Because personal code output never has any value once someone is a manager
Because a modest lift applied across every person on the team compounds to more total output than one person's individual share, even though the team-wide lift is much harder to see at a glance
Because code written by managers doesn't count toward the company's metrics
There's no reason -- personal output is always more valuable
items.explanation: The multiplier framing is about total value, not visibility. A distributed gain across a whole team is real and often larger, even when it's much harder to point to than a single merged PR.

items.prompt: Does this unit argue that management is a "harder" or "more advanced" version of being an individual contributor?
choices: Yes -- management is objectively the harder job and the natural next step for any strong IC
No -- they are different jobs requiring different skills; being excellent at one doesn't automatically transfer to the other, in either direction
Yes, but only at large companies
No -- management is actually an easier job than being an IC
items.explanation: The unit is explicit: this isn't a claim that one role is harder or better than the other. They're different jobs. A team's best engineer is not automatically its best manager, and vice versa.
items.reference:
Not a hierarchy

Peer IC and manager: different jobs, different skills
No Not "management is harder/better"
X Skill in one doesn't automatically transfer to the other

Why: treating promotion as an automatic reward for technical excellence sets both the new manager and their team up for a rough transition.
items.learnMore:
Different jobs, not a ranked ladder

This unit is explicit that management isn't framed as a harder or more prestigious version of being an IC -- it's a genuinely different job requiring a different, separately-built skill set.

A team's best engineer is not automatically its best manager, in the same way a great manager isn't automatically a great engineer. Neither direction of transfer is guaranteed.

Common mistake

Treating a promotion into management as a reward for past technical excellence, with no acknowledgment that the role itself has fundamentally changed and requires new skills.

items.prompt: What is the practical shift this unit asks a new manager to make?
choices: Work more hours than they did as an IC

Measure their own success by team output and team growth, not personal output, and deliberately build the specific skills (delegation, coaching, unblocking, prioritization across others' work) that requires
Stop doing any technical work permanently, starting day one
Delegate literally every task without exception
items.explanation: The unit's practical conclusion is a shift in what you measure yourself against -- team output and growth instead of personal output -- paired with deliberately building the new skills that support requires, not a blanket rule against doing any technical work.
items.reference:
Old question

What did I personally produce this week?

New question

Is my team more capable and clear than a month ago?

Why: the first question is familiar and fast-feedback; the second is the one that actually measures the job.
items.learnMore:
Measuring success by the right output

The practical shift this unit asks for is measuring your own success by team output and team growth, not personal output -- and deliberately building the specific new skills (delegation, coaching, unblocking, cross-person prioritization) that requires.

This isn't a one-time realization -- it's a standing discipline, because the pull back toward the old, familiar question doesn't go away after the first month.

Common mistake

Assuming that simply knowing this framework intellectually is the same as consistently applying it under weekly pressure. Recognizing the trap and resisting it in the moment are different skills.

items.learnMore:
The extra term in the manager's equation

The manager equation has a term the IC equation doesn't: how well-supported each person is. Unclear priorities, missing context, being blocked on a decision only the manager can make, or lacking coaching on a skill gap all directly multiply down every team member's effective output.

Closing those support gaps is the actual job now, even though -- unlike code -- it has no direct, personally-attributable output of its own.

Common mistake

Treating 'support' as a soft, optional extra rather than a multiplicative term that determines how much of the team's raw effort and skill actually converts into real output.

Because addition is mathematically simpler to explain
Because only junior team members are affected by support at all
items.explanation: A multiplicative relationship captures that poor support can gate output to near zero regardless of someone's raw effort and skill -- a blocked, unclear engineer's talent doesn't convert into results, which an additive model would understate.

items.prompt: Per L2's skill comparison table, why doesn't "being right" (a strong IC trait) transfer directly into effective management?
choices: Being right is equally valuable in both roles with no meaningful difference

The manager's job increasingly requires being willing to be visibly wrong in ways that make it safe for reports to disagree and take risks -- directly in tension with the IC habit of demonstrating competence through having the right answer
Managers are never expected to be technically correct about anything
This only matters for managers of very large teams
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames this as a tension, not just a gap: the instinct that made someone a strong IC (being right, having the answer) can actively work against the different skill the management role needs (creating psychological safety for others to be wrong and take risks).
items.reference:
IC instinct

Be right; demonstrate competence with the right answer

Manager skill

Be willing to be visibly wrong so reports feel safe to disagree and take risks

Why: these two instincts are in direct tension, not just unrelated skills.
items.learnMore:
"Being right" doesn't transfer

As an IC, demonstrating competence by having the right answer is a core, rewarded habit. As a manager, the job increasingly requires the opposite instinct: being willing to be publicly wrong in ways that model it's safe for reports to disagree, take risks, and be wrong themselves.

This is one of the clearest examples in the unit of a skill that doesn't just fail to transfer, but actively works against the new role if left unexamined.

Common mistake

Assuming a manager who's frequently visibly wrong is failing at the job. The point isn't accuracy for its own sake -- it's whether the team feels safe disagreeing and taking risks.

items.prompt: A manager who always has the correct technical answer, and always states it first in team discussions, might unintentionally be undermining what per L2's framework?

The company's budget for the team
The manager's own technical credibility
items.explanation: L2's point is that the IC habit of demonstrating competence through correctness is in tension with the manager's need to make it safe for others to be wrong -- always leading with the right answer can quietly signal that mistakes aren't welcome.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, why doesn't being excellent at writing clear code guarantee someone is good at giving feedback on someone else's code?
choices: It does guarantee it -- the skills are identical
Feedback requires framing that lands without demotivating the recipient -- a different communication skill from code clarity itself
Feedback is never actually necessary if the code is good
Only senior engineers are capable of giving feedback
items.explanation: L2 lists this as one of the clearest examples of a skill that doesn't transfer 1:1 -- code clarity and feedback delivery share some technical judgment but require genuinely different communication skills.
items.reference:
IC skill

Writing clear code

Manager skill

Writing clear, actionable feedback about someone else's code and choices

Why: feedback requires framing that lands without demotivating -- a different communication skill entirely from writing code well.
items.learnMore:
Feedback is a separate skill from code quality

Writing clear code and writing clear feedback about someone else's code are not the same skill, even though both involve technical judgment. Feedback additionally requires framing that lands without demotivating the person receiving it.

A manager who writes excellent code personally has no guarantee they can deliver hard feedback well -- it has to be built as its own skill, just like the other manager-column skills in L2's table.

Common mistake

Assuming that because someone writes very clear code, they'll automatically write (or deliver) clear feedback about someone else's code. The two draw on overlapping but distinct skills.

The report is simply too sensitive to receive any feedback

A manager who writes excellent code personally has no guarantee they can deliver hard feedback well -- it has to be built as its own skill, just like the other manager-column skills in L2's table.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, why is prioritizing across a team's work a different skill from prioritizing your own backlog as an IC?
choices: It's exactly the same skill, just applied to more tickets
It requires visibility into other people's partially-visible work and judgment about trade-offs affecting people other than yourself -- visibility and judgment the IC role never demanded
Team prioritization is always less important than personal prioritization
Only the most senior managers ever need to prioritize across a team
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that this requires visibility and judgment the IC role never demanded -- you can fully see your own backlog, but you only partially see everyone else's, and the trade-offs now affect other people's time and priorities.
items.reference:
IC skill

Prioritizing your own backlog

Manager skill

Prioritizing across several people's conflicting, partially-visible work

Why: this requires visibility and judgment the IC role never demanded -- you can't see everyone's full picture the way you could see your own.
items.learnMore:
Prioritizing one backlog vs. several

Prioritizing your own backlog only requires visibility into your own work and judgment about your own trade-offs. Prioritizing across several people's work requires visibility into work you didn't do and don't fully see, plus judgment about trade-offs that affect other people's time, not just your own.

This is why cross-team or cross-person prioritization conversations (like Path B's Week 3 in L3) are genuinely uncomfortable and unfamiliar even for a manager who was excellent at managing their own workload as an IC.

Common mistake

Assuming that because someone was great at prioritizing their own sprint as an IC, prioritizing across a whole team's conflicting work will come naturally. It requires visibility and judgment the IC role never actually demanded.

items.prompt: In L3, Path B's manager has uncomfortable political conversations with other teams in Week 3 to resolve priority ambiguity. Why is this specifically a manager-level skill rather than something any senior IC could do instead?
choices: Because ICs are legally prohibited from talking to other teams
Because it requires visibility and standing across teams' partially-visible priorities that an IC's own-backlog prioritization skill never built or required
Because political conversations are always easy for anyone with enough seniority
It isn't actually a manager-level skill -- any team member could do it equally well
items.explanation: Resolving priority ambiguity across teams requires the kind of cross-person visibility and standing that only comes with the manager role -- an IC's skill at prioritizing their own backlog doesn't transfer to that broader, partially-visible landscape.
items.reference:
IC skill

Prioritizing your own backlog

Manager skill

Prioritizing across several people's conflicting, partially-visible work

Why: this requires visibility and judgment the IC role never demanded -- you can't see everyone's full picture the way you could see your own.
items.learnMore:
Prioritizing one backlog vs. several

Prioritizing your own backlog only requires visibility into your own work and judgment about your own trade-offs. Prioritizing across several people's work requires visibility into work you didn't do and don't fully see, plus judgment about trade-offs that affect other people's time, not just your own.

This is why cross-team or cross-person prioritization conversations (like Path B's Week 3 in L3) are genuinely uncomfortable and unfamiliar even for a manager who was excellent at managing their own workload as an IC.

Common mistake

Assuming that because someone was great at prioritizing their own sprint as an IC, prioritizing across a whole team's conflicting work will come naturally. It requires visibility and judgment the IC role never actually demanded.

items.prompt: Per L2's closing section, what question should replace "what did I personally produce this week" for a manager's self-assessment?
choices: How many meetings did I attend this week?
Is my team more capable, more unblocked, and more clear on priorities than they were a month ago -- including in areas I didn't personally touch?
How many of my direct reports like me personally?
How much did I delegate this week, regardless of outcome?
items.explanation: L2 states this explicitly as the practical consequence of the multiplier-of-many framing -- team capability and clarity over time, not personal weekly output, including outcomes the manager didn't personally drive.
items.reference:
Wrong question

What did I personally produce this week?

Right question

Is my team more capable, unblocked, and clear than a month ago?

Why: the right question is harder to answer and slower to show results -- exactly why it's easy to substitute the familiar one instead.
items.learnMore:
The self-assessment question that actually matters

L2's practical conclusion: a manager's self-assessment shouldn't be "what did I personally produce this week" -- it should be whether the team is more capable, more unblocked, and more clear on priorities than a month ago, including in areas the manager didn't personally touch.

The second question is deliberately harder to answer and slower to show results, which is exactly why the faster, more familiar first question is so easy to substitute in its place without noticing.

Common mistake

Answering the easier, faster-feedback question (personal output) and treating it as if it answers the harder, slower one (team capability) -- they measure genuinely different things.

items.prompt: Per L3's first failure mode, why is it risky to judge a new manager's effectiveness by looking at any single week's visible output?
choices: Because visible output should always be the primary measure of management effectiveness

Because Path B's manager produced LESS visible personal output every single week than Path A's, even though Path B produced better team-level outcomes over the month -- a week-by-week IC-style read would score the wrong path higher
Because weekly output is impossible to measure in any management role
Because new managers should not be evaluated at all during their first quarter
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes this trap: Path B's coaching, delegation, and difficult conversations produce little to no manager-attributed output in any given week, while Path A's personal design doc is immediately visible -- the real difference only becomes legible in the team's trajectory over the full month, not in any single week's activity.
items.reference:
The trap in judging by the week

A Path A: visible design doc, every single week
B Path B: little visible output, most weeks
Win Path B's team capability wins over the full month

Why: the real difference is only legible in the team's month-long trajectory, not in any single week's activity log.
items.learnMore:
Why weekly output is a misleading measure

Path B's coaching, delegation, and difficult conversations produce little to no manager-attributed output in any given week. Path A's personal design doc is immediately visible the same week it's written.

A week-by-week, IC-style read of either path in isolation would score Path A higher every time -- the real difference between the two only becomes legible in the team's trajectory over the full month, not in any single week's activity.

Common mistake

Evaluating a new manager's first few weeks by counting visible personal deliverables. That measure will consistently favor the retreat-to-IC-work pattern over the pattern that's actually better for the team long-term.

items.prompt: Per L3's second failure mode, does this unit argue that a good manager should stop doing any hands-on technical work entirely?
choices: Yes -- any personal technical contribution by a manager is always a mistake

No -- the shift is in DEFAULT behavior under ambiguity (delegate and coach first) and what fills most of the time, not an absolute prohibition; losing all technical touch can itself cost the credibility and judgment the role still needs
Yes, but only for managers of teams larger than ten people
No, managers should split their time exactly 50/50 between technical work and management work in all cases
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against over-correcting into zero hands-on work -- the argument is about where the majority of time and the default response to ambiguity goes, not a claim that any technical involvement by a manager is inherently wrong.
items.reference:
Wrong takeaway

Managers should do zero hands-on technical work, ever

Actual takeaway

Shift the DEFAULT under ambiguity toward delegate-and-coach; don't lose all technical touch

Why: a manager fully out of touch with the technical work can lose the credibility and judgment the role still needs.
items.learnMore:
Not an argument for zero technical involvement

L3's second failure mode is explicit: the goal isn't zero personal technical contribution forever. A manager who's completely lost touch with the technical work can lose the credibility and judgment the role still needs.

What actually shifts is the default behavior under ambiguity -- delegate and coach first -- and what fills the majority of the manager's time, not an absolute prohibition on ever writing code again.

Common mistake

Over-correcting from Path A's mistake into never touching technical work again. That's presented explicitly as its own failure mode, not the intended lesson.

Yes, but only for managers who were exceptionally strong ICs

items.explanation: L3 is explicit that this is a recurring pull, not a one-time first-month mistake -- every new moment of uncertainty in the management role recreates the same temptation to retreat to familiar, comfortable work.
items.reference:
Not a one-time first-month mistake

Loop The pull toward familiar IC work doesn't expire after month one
Again Every new moment of uncertainty recreates it
Ongoing Requires a standing discipline, not a one-time fix

Why: if it's treated as a first-month mistake you simply grow out of, the retreat can quietly recur every time a new uncertain situation shows up.
items.learnMore:
A standing discipline, not a phase

L3's third failure mode warns against treating the IC-retreat pattern as something limited to a manager's first month on the job. The comfort of familiar, fast-feedback IC work doesn't go away once someone has been managing for a year.

Every future moment of uncertainty in the role creates the same pull back toward the familiar work -- which is why resisting it has to be an ongoing discipline, not a phase that's simply grown out of with tenure.

Common mistake

Assuming that once a manager has successfully navigated their first uncertain month, the retreat-to-IC-work risk is permanently behind them. New uncertain situations keep recreating the same pull.

items.explanation: L3 places real responsibility on the organizational framing of the promotion itself, not just the individual manager -- treating promotion as pure reward, with no explicit acknowledgment or teaching of the new role's skills, sets even a talented person up for a rough transition.

Framing as role change

items.learnMore:

items.explanation: L3 shows the trade-off directly: fixing it personally is faster and feels productive in the moment, but the junior engineer keeps needing the same kind of unblocking; coaching them through it is slower this week but the gap actually closes.

Coach through it

items.learnMore:
Week 2: fixing vs. coaching

In Week 2, Path A's manager personally fixes the junior engineer's bug in twenty minutes because it's faster than sitting with them. Path B's manager sits with the engineer, asks questions rather than supplying the answer, and helps them find the fix themselves -- slower in the moment.

The payoff shows up the following week: Path A's junior engineer gets "unblocked" the same way multiple times without the underlying gap closing; Path B's junior engineer independently solves a similar problem later because the actual skill gap closed.

Common mistake

Judging Week 2 in isolation, where Path A's fix looks strictly better (faster, unblocked sooner). The real payoff of Path B's slower approach only shows up in whether the same problem recurs afterward.
